Abstract.

Vladimir Shpilrain and Jie-Tai Yu have asked for an effective algorithm to decide if two elements of ℂ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] are related by an automorphism of ℂ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{C}}[x,y]. We describe here an efficient algorithm, due to the second author, that decides this question and finds the automorphism if it exists. We also discuss some examples related to work of Shpilrain and Yu. Part of the purpose of this paper is to advertise the use of splice diagrams in studying ℂ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{C}}[x,y].

Key words and phrases: 
polynomial automorphism
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
12Y05, 14H50

1. Introduction

We give an efficient algorithmic answer to the following problem, which was posed by Shpilrain and Yu [15] and resolved by them in special cases. The algorithm is due to the second author in [19], where it is described in terms of Newton polygons. Here we describe it in terms of splice diagrams.

Problem 1.1.

Given polynomials f,g∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y], decide if there exists a polynomial automorphism ϕ∈Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] with f​ϕ=gf\phi=g and find ϕ\phi if it exists.

As we discuss in the final section, ℂ{\mathbb{C}} could be replaced by any field, although in finite characteristic the description in terms of splice diagrams given here would need some modification.

Any ϕ∈Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] induces a polynomial bijection ℂ2→ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{2} (which we also call ϕ\phi) and vice versa. From this point of view, the problem asks for a polynomial bijection ϕ:ℂ2→ℂ2\phi\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{2} which makes the diagram

commutative. We shall use the terminology “ff is right-equivalent to gg” for this. From a topological point of view it is also natural to ask about “right-left equivalence”, which asks for polynomial bijections ϕ:ℂ2→ℂ2\phi\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{2} and ψ:ℂ→ℂ\psi\colon{\mathbb{C}}\to{\mathbb{C}} making

commutative (ψ\psi is an affine map ψ⁡(z)=a​z+b\psi(z)=az+b with a≠0a\neq 0). Our results apply also to this. We shall use the abbreviation “equivalence” to mean right-equivalence.

Shpilrain and Yu say ff and gg in ℂ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] are “isomorphic” if the curves f⁡(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 and g⁡(x,y)=0g(x,y)=0 are isomorphic as affine schemes; that is, their rings of functions ℂ⁡[x,y]/(f){\mathbb{C}}[x,y]/(f) and ℂ⁡[x,y]/(g){\mathbb{C}}[x,y]/(g) are isomorphic. In the final section we discuss some of their examples, and additional examples motivated from their work, of isomorphic but non-equivalent polynomials.

We first recall the structure of the automorphism group Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y]. It has two subgroups

A\displaystyle A :=Affℂ2={(x,y)↦(ax+by+s,cx+dy+t):a,b,c,d,s,t∈ℂ}\displaystyle:=\operatorname{Aff}{\mathbb{C}}^{2}=\{(x,y)\mapsto(ax+by+s,cx+dy+t):a,b,c,d,s,t\in{\mathbb{C}}\}
B\displaystyle B :={(x,y)↦(ax+g(y),dy+t):g(y)∈ℂ[y],a,d,t∈ℂ}\displaystyle:=\{(x,y)\mapsto(ax+g(y),dy+t):g(y)\in{\mathbb{C}}[y],a,d,t\in{\mathbb{C}}\}

BB is called the “Jonquière subgroup”.

Theorem 1.2 (Jung [7], 1942)

Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] is generated by its subgroups AA and BB.

This theorem implies that any ϕ∈Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] has an expression

ϕ=ϕ1​ϕ2​…​ϕn\phi=\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\dots\phi_{n}

with ϕi\phi_{i} in AA for ii even and in BB for ii odd or vice versa. Moreover, we may assume that if n>1n>1 then no ϕi\phi_{i} is in A∩BA\cap B. We call such an expression normal form.

If each ϕi\phi_{i} in BB is actually in the subgroup of triangular automorphisms

T:={(x,y)↦(x+g⁡(y),y):g⁡(y)∈ℂ⁡[y]}.T:=\{(x,y)\mapsto(x+g(y),y):g(y)\in{\mathbb{C}}[y]\}.

we shall speak of strict normal form. We can always change a normal form representation with n>1n>1 to strict normal form by applying changes of the form: replace ϕi\phi_{i} and ϕi+1\phi_{i+1} by ϕi​χ\phi_{i}\chi and χ−1​ϕi+1\chi^{-1}\phi_{i+1} with χ∈A∩B\chi\in A\cap B.

The following theorem is stated in slightly different form in [19].

Theorem 1.3 (Wightwick [19])

Suppose f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] is a non-constant polynomial and ϕ∈Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y]. Suppose ϕ=ϕ1​ϕ2​…​ϕn\phi=\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\dots\phi_{n} is a normal form expression for ϕ\phi, and put fi=f​ϕ1​ϕ2​…​ϕif_{i}=f\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\dots\phi_{i} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, and f0=ff_{0}=f. Then the sequence of degrees deg⁡(fi)\operatorname{deg}(f_{i}) satisfies

deg(f0)≥⋯≥deg(fk)≤⋯≤deg(fn),for some 0≤k≤n.\operatorname{deg}(f_{0})\geq\dots\geq\operatorname{deg}(f_{k})\leq\dots\leq\operatorname{deg}(f_{n}),\quad\text{for some }0\leq k\leq n.

Moreover, there is at most one ϕi∈B\phi_{i}\in B for which deg⁡(fi−1)=deg⁡(fi)\operatorname{deg}(f_{i-1})=\operatorname{deg}(f_{i}), and if this happens then deg⁡(fi)\operatorname{deg}(f_{i}) is the minimal degree deg⁡(fk)\operatorname{deg}(f_{k}).

This theorem implies the result (van der Kulk [9], 1953) that Aut⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]\operatorname{Aut}{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] is the amalgamated free product of AA and BB, amalgamated along A∩BA\cap B. For if not, there would be a non-trivial normal form representation of ϕ=1\phi=1 with ϕ1∈B\phi_{1}\in B, and applying the theorem with this ϕ\phi to f=xf=x gives a contradiction.

The theorem clearly implies that nn is at most 2​(deg⁡(f0)+deg⁡(fn))+12(\operatorname{deg}(f_{0})+\operatorname{deg}(f_{n}))+1. It is also easy to see that that each ϕi\phi_{i} has degree at most max⁡(deg⁡(fi−1),deg⁡(fi))\max(\operatorname{deg}(f_{i-1}),\operatorname{deg}(f_{i})) (this also follows from the proof in [19]). This already implies an algorithm for Problem 1.1, since it implies a bound of N4​N+1N^{4N+1} on the degree of the automorphism ϕ\phi with N=max⁡(deg⁡(f),deg⁡(g))N=\max(\operatorname{deg}(f),\operatorname{deg}(g)), so finding ϕ\phi amounts to solving a system of algebraic equations in the coefficients of this automorphism, for which computational techniques are known. However, we promised an efficient algorithm, and this algorithm would be inefficient even if this bound on deg⁡(ϕ)\operatorname{deg}(\phi) were much improved (as it can be).

We will describe the efficient algorithm in terms of the splice diagrams introduced in the book [6]. They were used there to describe the local topology of plane curve singularities. Later, in [11], they were used to discuss the global topology of polynomial maps f:ℂ2→ℂf\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{C}}, which is what interests us here.

2. Splice diagrams

Associated to a fiber f−1​(c)⊂ℂ2f^{-1}(c)\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2} of a non-constant polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] is a combinatorial invariant: the splice diagram Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) for f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c). It is a tree with certain numerical and other decorations on it. There are finitely many values of cc for which this diagram differs from its generic value. The generic diagram is called the regular splice diagram for ff, denoted Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f). As we shall describe, Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) encodes behaviour at infinity of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c). Therefore, for the finitely many cc for which Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) is not regular we speak of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) being irregular at infinity or having “singularities at infinity.”

For example, the so called Briançon polynomial,

f⁡(x,y)=x2​(1+x​y)4+3​x​(1+x​y)3+(3−83​x)​(1+x​y)2−4​(1+x​y)+y,f(x,y)=x^{2}(1+xy)^{4}+3x(1+xy)^{3}+(3-\frac{8}{3}x)(1+xy)^{2}-4(1+xy)+y,

discussed in detail in [3], has regular splice diagram:

We explain such diagrams in greater detail below, but first we explain why they are useful invariants.

First, Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) is easily computable (by hand; or explicit computer code is also available in Magma [4]). In fact, Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) is simply a graphical representation of the exponents of the topologically relevant terms in the Puiseux expansions at infinity of f⁡(x,y)=cf(x,y)=c, and Newton already knew how to compute Puiseux expansions. The regular splice diagram Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) is easily derived purely combinatorially from Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) (see [13]), so one does not need to know a regular value of ff to find Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f).

Second, each Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) individually is an invariant under equivalence of ff, while the collection of them is an invariant under right-left equivalence (in particular, the regular splice diagram Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) is invariant under right-left equivalence of ff).

Actually, splice diagrams exist in two versions, the rooted and unrooted splice diagrams, and the above are the unrooted versions. The rooted splice diagrams will be denoted Γ∙​(f−1​(c))\Gamma_{\bullet}(f^{-1}(c)) and Γ∙​(f)\Gamma_{\bullet}(f) respectively. For the above examples the rooted diagrams differ from the unrooted ones by the addition of a root vertex (drawn as a filled dot “∙\bullet” with adjacent numeric weights 11) in the center of the edge with weights −3,−1-3,-1.

We usually omit edge weights 11. For example, the rooted splice diagram for Briançon’s polynomial is therefore

The unrooted splice diagrams encode topology of f:ℂ2→ℂf\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{C}}, while the rooted splice diagrams encode the same topology together with its relationship to a generic line in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}. Thus, the rooted splice diagram is not an invariant of equivalence, since the concept of generic line is not invariant under polynomial automorphisms. The topological meaning of these diagrams is detailed in [11] and surveyed in [12]. We will here give a brief description of the algebraic meaning. See also [5] for an extended survey and [18] for details of how to compute splice diagrams using Newton polygons.

We first describe the general structure of the splice diagrams that arise in our situation (the splice diagrams used to describe plane curve singularities are similar except that edge determinants are positive in Item 2.1.5).

2.1. Properties of splice diagrams

2.1.1.

Each arrowhead in the splice diagram corresponds to a branch at infinity of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) (a branch at infinity can be taken to be a component of the intersection of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) with the complement of a large ball in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}).

2.1.2.

Each edge emanating from the root vertex corresponds to a point at infinity of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) (a point at infinity is a point of intersection of the closure of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) in ℂ​P2{\mathbb{C}}P^{2} with the line at infinity ℂ​P1{\mathbb{C}}P^{1}). All edge weights adjacent to the root vertex are 11.

2.1.3.

Any other vertex of the splice diagram is either

  • •

    a leaf: a non-arrowhead vertex of valency 1. It has no adjacent weights.

  • •

    a node: a non-arrowhead vertex of valency ≥2\geq 2. It has pairwise coprime integer weights associated to its adjacent edges.

Each edge will thus have a weight at its near end, seen from the node, and may have a weight at its far end. We call weights “near” or “far” correspondingly.

2.1.4.

All near weights are positive and at most one of the near weights at any node differs from 11 (edge weights 1 are usually omitted in the diagram). A far weight can be any integer.

2.1.5.

The edge determinant of an edge connecting two nodes (one of which may be the root vertex) is the product of the two weights on the edge minus the product of the weights adjacent to the edge. All edge determinants are negative. For example, in the rooted diagram above the three edge determinants are, from left to right, −3−2=−5-3-2=-5, −1−2=−3-1-2=-3, and −7−(−1×2×3)=−1-7-(-1\times 2\times 3)=-1.

2.1.6.

(Reduction 1) Any edge with edge weight 11 leading to a leaf may be deleted (with the leaf).

2.1.7.

(Reduction 2) Any node (other than the root vertex) of valency 22 may be removed, and the adjacent edges coalesced into a single edge.

Definition 2.1.

A diagram is reduced if neither Reduction 1 nor Reduction 2 can be applied to it. In particular, all non-root nodes have valency ≥3\geq 3.

We will assume diagrams are reduced unless otherwise stated, and the notations Γ∙​(f−1​(c))\Gamma_{\bullet}(f^{-1}(c)), Γ∙​(f−1​(c))\Gamma_{\bullet}(f^{-1}(c)), Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)), and Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) will always mean reduced diagrams.

Here, the unrooted splice diagram Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) or Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) is the result of changing the root vertex of the corresponding rooted diagram to an ordinary vertex and then reducing by Reductions 1 and/or 2 as necessary. However, there is an exceptional case described at the end of this section, where a further reduction must be done to eliminate a vanishing edge determinant.

2.4. Non-reduced fibers

As above, if a polynomial ff has non-reduced fibers then weights at arrowheads of the splice diagram are used to indicate multiplicities of components of such a fiber. Such a diagram is of course an irregular diagram.

3. Invariants from splice diagrams

Much of this section is not essential for what follows, but the invariants encoded in splice diagrams are often helpful in computing them, since they give strong numerical constraints.

Given a vertex vv of a splice diagram Γ\Gamma, the linking coefficient at vv (also called multiplicity at vv) is the sum over arrowheads ww of Γ\Gamma:

ℓv=∑wℓ⁡(v,w),\ell_{v}=\sum_{w}\ell(v,w),

3.1. Properties relating to linking coefficients

3.1.1.

The degree of a polynomial is always the linking coefficient ℓ∙\ell_{\bullet} at the root vertex.

3.1.2.

A splice diagram is regular if and only if it has no negative linking coefficients and the fiber in question is reduced (i.e., there are no multiplicity weights at arrowheads).

3.1.3.

A polynomial has fibers with irregular splice diagrams if and only if the regular splice diagram has at least one zero linking coefficient. Each irregular diagram determines the regular one and the regular one strongly constrains the number and form of the irregular ones ([13]).

3.1.4.

The Euler characteristic of the generic fiber of ff is

χr​e​g:=∑v∈vert⁡Γ⁡(f)(2−δv)​ℓv,\chi_{reg}:=\sum_{v\in\operatorname{vert}\Gamma(f)}(2-\delta_{v})\ell_{v},

where vert⁡Γ⁡(f)\operatorname{vert}\Gamma(f) is the set of non-arrowhead vertices of Γ⁡(f)\Gamma(f) and δv\delta_{v} is valency of vertex vv (number of edges at vv).

3.1.5.

For any c∈ℂc\in{\mathbb{C}} define the Milnor number at infinity of f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) as

λc:=∑v∈vert⁡Γ⁡(f−1​(c))ℓv<0(2−δv)​ℓv,\lambda_{c}:=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{\scriptstyle v\in\vert\splice(f^{-1}(c))}{\scriptstyle\ell_v<0}}(2-\delta_{v})\ell_{v},

so λc=0\lambda_{c}=0 unless Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) is irregular. Moreover, if f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) is a reduced fiber, define its total Milnor number as the sum of Milnor numbers:

μc:=∑p∈f−1​(p)μp\mu_{c}:=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(p)}\mu_{p}

(since μp=0\mu_{p}=0 at a non-singular point, this is a finite sum). Then the Euler characteristic of a reduced fiber f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) is given by

χ⁡(f−1​(c))=μc+∑v∈vert⁡Γ⁡(f−1​(c))(2−δv)​ℓv=μc+λc+χr​e​g.\chi(f^{-1}(c))=\mu_{c}+\sum_{v\in\operatorname{vert}\Gamma(f^{-1}(c))}(2-\delta_{v})\ell_{v}=\mu_{c}+\lambda_{c}+\chi_{reg}.

3.1.6.

(Suzuki [17]) For any ff one has 1−χr​e​g=∑c∈ℂ(χ⁡(f−1​(c)−χr​e​g)CLOSE1-\chi_{reg}=\sum_{c\in{\mathbb{C}}}\bigl(\chi(f^{-1}(c)-\chi_{reg}\bigr), so if all fibers of ff are reduced (i.e., ff has only isolated singularities) then

1−χr​e​g=∑c∈ℂ(μc+λc).1-\chi_{reg}=\sum_{c\in{\mathbb{C}}}(\mu_{c}+\lambda_{c}).

In the formulae of Items 3.1.4. and 3.1.5. one can use either the rooted or unrooted diagram (in fact the the formulae do not need reduced diagrams).

For any polynomial, as soon as singularities and “singularities at infinity” are found contributing sufficient μc\mu_{c} and λc\lambda_{c} to satisfy Suzuki’s formula, one knows that all non-generic fibers have been found. For example, for Briançon’s polynomial, Items 3.1.4. and 3.1.5. give:

χr​e​g=−3;λ0=1,λ−16/3=3.\chi_{reg}=-3;\quad\lambda_{0}=1,\quad\lambda_{-16/3}=3.

These already satisfy Suzuki’s formula, so the fibers f−1​(0)f^{-1}(0) and f−1(−16/3)f^{-1}(-16/3) are indeed the only fibers with singularities at infinity and there are no “finite” singularities. Briançon’s polynomial was the first non-singular polynomial discovered that also has all fibers connected [3], although Briançon constructed it for a different purpose.

{(a,b)∈ℝ2:xayb is a monomial of f}∪{(0,0)}.\{(a,b)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}:x^{a}y^{b}\text{ is a monomial of }f\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.

(This would better be called the “regular Newton polygon” and the adjective “regular” dropped if (0,0)(0,0) is not explicitly added, but we shall only use this version.)

5. Algorithms

5.1. Linear positioning

We first perform a linear automorphism to put points at infinity of ff in “standard position”.

Write f⁡(x,y)=f0​(x,y)+f1​(x,y)+⋯+fN​(x,y)f(x,y)=f_{0}(x,y)+f_{1}(x,y)+\dots+f_{N}(x,y) where fi​(x,y)f_{i}(x,y) is the homogeneous part of degree ii. The points at infinity for any fiber f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) are the points of vanishing of the linear factors of fN​(x,y)f_{N}(x,y). By a linear change of coordinates one of them can be put at [x:y]=[1:0][x{:}y]=[1{:}0] and, if there is more than one, another at [x:y]=[0:1][x{:}y]=[0{:}1]. For the Newton polygon this means that the part lying on the line x+y=Nx+y=N either does not include the points (0,N)(0,N) and (N,0)(N,0) or consists only of the former point.

We shall assume from now on that ff has been positioned in this way.

5.2. Reduction of degree

A reduced rooted splice diagram is minimal if it results from the reduced unrooted splice diagram by placing a root vertex either at an existing vertex or on an existing edge. We also call the exceptional diagrams discussed in Subsection 2.3 minimal.

Proposition 5.1

Assume we have applied a linear automorphism as above so [1:0][1{:}0] is a point at infinity for f⁡(x,y)f(x,y). Then, if the reduced rooted splice diagram for f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) is not minimal, there is an automorphism of the form (x,y)↦(x−c​yq,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-cy^{q},y) which reduces the degree of ff.

Proof.

If the reduced rooted splice diagram is not minimal, the root vertex has just one edge emanating and that edge has far weight 11. In terms of the Newton polygon this means that for some q>1q>1 there is a segment of slope −q-q touching the yy-axis (qq is the near weight at the vertex adjacent to the root).

Then f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) has the form

f⁡(x,y)=b​ya​∏k=1s(x+ck​yq)rk+∑q​i+j<q​S+aci​j​xi​yj,where ​S=∑k=1srk.f(x,y)=by^{a}\prod_{k=1}^{s}(x+c_{k}y^{q})^{r_{k}}+\sum_{qi+j<qS+a}c_{ij}x^{i}y^{j},\quad\text{where }S=\sum_{k=1}^{s}r_{k}.

Composing ff with any of the automorphisms (x,y)↦(x−ck​yq,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-c_{k}y^{q},y) will reduce the degree of ff. ∎

By iterating the procedure of the above proposition we can apply automorphisms to f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) until its reduced rooted splice diagram is minimal. This procedure reduces the degree of ff. Thus some minimal rooted splice diagram corresponds to an automorphic image of ff of least possible degree. However, there may be several minimal rooted diagrams, and not all of them will give the absolute minimal degree among automorphic images of ff.

In any case, we assume from now on that Γ∙​(f)\Gamma_{\bullet}(f) is minimal.

5.3. Changing reduced splice diagram

A reduced unrooted splice diagram Γ=Γ​(f−1​(c))\Gamma=\Gamma(f^{-1}(c)) may have several places where one can put a root vertex to make it into a rooted splice diagram. In [11] it is shown how to realise each resulting rooted splice diagram as Γ∙​((f​ϕ)−1​(c))\Gamma_{\bullet}\bigl((f\phi)^{-1}(c)\bigr) for a suitable polynomial automorphism ϕ\phi. Since this is an essential part of our algorithm we describe it here.

We will assume Γ\Gamma is non-exceptional since each exceptional Γ\Gamma has a unique minimal rooted splice diagram (see Subsection 2.3).

We first describe how to find all potential root vertices for Γ\Gamma. Choose one possible root vertex. Consider a simple path from this vertex to another vertex with the properties:

  • •

    The edge weights on the path are all positive except maybe at the very end of the path;

  • •

    If an edge weight adjacent to the path is >1>1 then it is the only edge weight >1>1 at its node. A node where this happens is called a contributing node (following [11]) and we say the path “passes” this contributing node. (If a path through a contributing node has the weight >1>1 on it rather than adjacent to it, we say it “goes through” the contributing node.)

Take the subgraph Γ0\Gamma_{0} of Γ\Gamma that is the union of all these paths. Each possible position for a root node lies at a vertex or on an edge of this subgraph. Their positions are found as follows. A directed path in Γ0\Gamma_{0} is a simple path starting at a vertex or edge midpoint and departing each node along it by an edge with maximal weight among the edge-weights of Γ\Gamma at that node. The condition of negative edge determinants implies that a maximal directed path will either start at a leaf, in the middle of an edge, or at a node with all adjacent weights 11 and it will end at a vertex with non-positive edge weight, an arrowhead, or at a contributing vertex. The starting points of maximal directed paths in Γ0\Gamma_{0} are the possible positions for root vertices. In fact every half-edge of Γ0\Gamma_{0} is on a unique maximal directed path, so these maximal directed paths give a flow on Γ0\Gamma_{0} and the possible root vertices are the sources of this flow (see [11]).

Any simple path in Γ0\Gamma_{0} will be a union of directed paths laid end-to-end with directions alternating. The direction can only change from forward to backward as we pass a contributing vertex and can only change from backward to forward as we go through a potential root vertex. We shall call two potential root vertices “adjacent” if the path between them goes through no other potential root vertex, so it changes direction exactly once, and this happens as it passes some contributing node. (The path may, however go through other contributing nodes without “passing” them—see Item 2. above.)

A typical path between adjacent potential root vertices is the path from ∙\bullet to ∗* in Figure 1 (the pi​jp_{ij} are greater than 11 and increase to the right in the graph). We are omitting vertices that are neither contributing nodes nor potential root vertices in this picture (they are all of valency at most 22 in Γ0\Gamma_{0}). The vertices at the left of the picture are pairwise adjacent potential root vertices.

If ff does have several minimal rooted splice diagrams we need to find automorphisms that move us from one to another. It suffices to move between adjacent potential root vertices.

Suppose the root of Γ∙​(f)\Gamma_{\bullet}(f) is at the top left in Figure 1. Let the rightward edge at that node correspond to the point [1:0][1{:}0] at infinity. Then the Newton polygon will have segments on its boundary with slopes −p11,…,−p1​j,…,−p21,…-p_{11},\dots,-{p_{1j}},\dots,-p_{21},\dots. There may be segments with other slopes corresponding to vertices of Γ∙​(f)\Gamma_{\bullet}(f) that are valency two in Γ0\Gamma_{0} and therefore not drawn in the figure or a segment of slope 1 coming from additional edges at vertex ∙\bullet. Suppose we want to move the root vertex to the position ∗*. This moves it past the contributing node vv with adjacent weight p1​jp_{1j}. The terms of f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) corresponding to the Newton polygon segment of slope −p1​j-p_{1j} give a polynomial xa​yb​∏i=1s(x+ci​yp1​j)rix^{a}y^{b}\prod_{i=1}^{s}(x+c_{i}y^{p_{1j}})^{r_{i}} with each factor (x+ci​yp1​j)ri(x+c_{i}y^{p_{1j}})^{r_{i}} corresponding to one of the relevant edges emerging to the left from vv. If the edge at vv towards ∗* is the one with index ii then the automorphism (x,y)↦(x−ci​yp1​j,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-c_{i}y^{p_{1j}},y) moves the root vertex as desired. However, the resulting diagram may need further automorphisms as in Subsection 5.2 to reduce it to a minimal diagram again (an automorphism that gives a minimal diagram will be of the form (x,y)↦(x−g⁡(y),y)(x,y)\mapsto(x-g(y),y) with g⁡(y)g(y) a polynomial with highest order term ci​yp1​jc_{i}y^{p_{1j}}). Moreover, the result may not be to move the root vertex to ∗*, but rather to some other of the potential roots to the left of vv via the ii-th edge out of vertex vv, for instance, the vertex above ∗* in the figure. But we can iterate the procedure to try to move from the new root to ∗*. Since each iteration involves a contributing vertex closer to ∗*, this iterative procedure eventually ends with our node at ∗*.

5.4. Comparing polynomials

Given two polynomials ff and gg in ℂ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{C}}[x,y], their (reduced unrooted) splice diagrams are likely to distinguish them if they are not equivalent (or even not right-left-equivalent), so the first thing to do is compute these and reduce them as above. Often ff and gg can be distinguished without computing the whole splice diagram, or they may be distinguished by an irregular splice diagram or by positions of singularities or of irregular fibers. We will just consider the regular splice diagram here.

We may thus assume that we have applied automorphisms to ff and gg so they have isomorphic rooted regular splice diagrams and these diagrams are minimal. After fixing gg, there may be several ways of introducing a root in the unrooted splice diagram for ff to make the diagrams isomorphic, and several isomorphisms, so there may be several cases to try. For each case we proceed as follows.

First, apply a linear automorphism as in subsection 5.1, if it exists, so that the points at infinity of ff and gg are the same for corresponding edges at the root vertices of Γ∙​(f)\Gamma_{\bullet}(f) and Γ∙​(g)\Gamma_{\bullet}(g). This automorphism will exist if there are three or less points at infinity, but it is uniquely determined up to scaling by three points, so if there are four or more points at infinity it may not exist, in which case there is no automorphism taking ff to gg (or even ff to α​g+β\alpha g+\beta with α,β∈ℂ\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{C}}) for the given isomorphism of splice diagrams.

Once points at infinity are matched, the problem of finding an automorphism, if it exists, taking ff to gg (or ff to some α​g+β\alpha g+\beta) for this particular isomorphism of splice diagrams reduces, by the following theorem, to solving simple equations in a very limited number of variables (α,β\alpha,\beta, and the coefficients of the ϕ\phi described in the theorem).

Theorem 5.2

Suppose f=f⁡(x,y)f=f(x,y) has minimal rooted splice diagram. Assume also that a point at infinity occurs at [1:0][1{:}0], and a second, if it exists, at [0:1][0{:}1], and that ff is not a polynomial in yy alone. Suppose ϕ\phi is an automorphism that does not move the root vertex of ff and does not move any point at infinity11 1 From an algebraic point of view, to say an automorphism moves neither the root vertex nor any point at infinity means that each branch at infinity of a generic fiber f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) should be at the same point at infinity before and after applying the automorphism.. Then

  • •

    If ff has one point at infinity then ϕ\phi is in the Jonquière subgroup BB, that is, it is of the form ϕ⁡(x,y)=(b​x+h⁡(y),d​y+t)\phi(x,y)=(bx+h(y),dy+t). The degree of hh is bounded by the absolute value of slope of the top segment of the Newton polygon boundary (in particular, deg⁡(h)≤deg⁡(f)\operatorname{deg}(h)\leq\operatorname{deg}(f)).

  • •

    If ff has two points at infinity then ϕ⁡(x,y)=(a​x+s,d​y+t)\phi(x,y)=(ax+s,dy+t).

  • •

    If ff has three or more points at infinity then ϕ⁡(x,y)=(a​x+s,a​y+t)\phi(x,y)=(ax+s,ay+t).

Proof.

The specific form of ϕ\phi described in the theorem is easily seen if ϕ\phi is affine, so assume it is not. Since the automorphism ϕ\phi does not change the splice diagram, it does not change the degree of ff (see Item 3.1.1 in Section 3). By Theorem 1.3, a normal form representation for the automorphism ϕ\phi involves exactly one factor from BB. We can thus write it as ϕ1∘ϕ2∘ϕ3\phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2}\circ\phi_{3}, with ϕ2∈B−A\phi_{2}\in B-A and ϕ1,ϕ3∈A\phi_{1},\phi_{3}\in A, but with no restriction on non-triviality of ϕ1,ϕ3\phi_{1},\phi_{3}. We can modify ϕ2\phi_{2} and ϕ3\phi_{3} to make ϕ2\phi_{2} triangular, say (x,y)↦(x+h⁡(y),y)(x,y)\mapsto(x+h(y),y) with deg⁡(h)>1\operatorname{deg}(h)>1. Denote fi=f​ϕ1​…​ϕif_{i}=f\phi_{1}\dots\phi_{i}. By Theorem 1.3, f,f1,f2,f3f,f_{1},f_{2},f_{3} all have the same degree NN say. Note that f1f_{1} has the same number of points at infinity as ff. If f1​(x,y)f_{1}(x,y) had a point at infinity other than [1:0][1{:}0] then it would have a monomial xa​yN−ax^{a}y^{N-a} with a>1a>1. Taking the largest such aa, it would follow that f2=f1​ϕ2f_{2}=f_{1}\phi_{2} has a monomial ya​deg⁡(h)+N−ay^{a\operatorname{deg}(h)+N-a} and thus has degree larger than NN. Thus f1f_{1} has just one point at infinity at [1:0][1{:}0], so ϕ1\phi_{1} fixes this point and is therefore in A∩BA\cap B. The same argument applied to f=f3​ψ3​ψ2​ψ1f=f_{3}\psi_{3}\psi_{2}\psi_{1} with ψi=ϕi−1\psi_{i}=\phi_{i}^{-1} shows ψ3∈A∩B\psi_{3}\in A\cap B so ϕ3∈A∩B\phi_{3}\in A\cap B. Thus ϕ∈B\phi\in B, as claimed.

The statement about the degree of h⁡(y)h(y) follows by noting that, if the slope of the top segment in the Newton polygon is −p/q-p/q and if deg⁡(h)>p/q\operatorname{deg}(h)>p/q then a monomial xN−r​q​yr​px^{N-rq}y^{rp} corresponding to the lowest point on this top segment of the Newton polygon for ff leads to a monomial y(N−r​q)​deg⁡(h)+r​py^{(N-rq)\operatorname{deg}(h)+rp} for f​ϕf\phi. Since (N−r​q)​deg⁡(h)+r​p>(N−r​q)​p/q+r​p=N​p/q>N(N-rq)\operatorname{deg}(h)+rp>(N-rq)p/q+rp=Np/q>N, this completes the proof. ∎

The Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki theorem ([1], [17]) says that if f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] has a non-singular contractible fibre then ff is a coordinate (meaning equivalent to xx). There are now many proofs of this, and they all proceed by (implicitly or explicitly) constructing the linear and triangular automorphism which together reduce the degree of ff. A rather different algorithm to recognise a coordinate is given in [14].

The fiber f−1​(1)f^{-1}(1) is also reducible, with a normal crossing singularity at (0,−1)(0,-1), but it is regular at infinity. The contributions from this singularity and the singularity at infinity of the fiber over 00 fulfil Suzuki’s formula (end of Section 3), so we see again that there are no other non-generic fibers.

This is just one example of a polynomial with all generic fibers isomorphic. Such polynomials are called isotrivial and have been classified (see Kaliman [8]).

6.5. Other fields

Our base field has been ℂ{\mathbb{C}} for convenience and to emphasize the geometric underpinnings for the approach. However, algebraic closure is certainly not essential since one can always perform computation in extension fields as necessary. The assumption of characteristic zero is also inessential for the algorithm: the proof of Theorem 1.3 in [19] goes through with no change and the algorithm, as described there without splice diagrams, also works. However, the theory of splice diagrams would need some modification in finite characteristic.
